oil.summary: Crude closed little changed on the day — WTI at $77.21 (-0.08%) and Brent at $82.50 (+0.01%) — but those flat prints mask a brutal week: both benchmarks shed roughly 8.5% as markets priced in a potential Strait of Hormuz breakthrough. RBOB was the standout loser, cratering 7.61% on the session and nearly 16% on the week. The intraday tape told the story: WTI opened at $80.10, briefly printed $82.33, then sold off sharply before partially recovering. Beneath the geopolitical de-escalation narrative, structural stress remains acute — ADNOC reported 15 vessel attacks with material operational impact and spent $1.3 billion on 11 supertankers to bolster export capacity. Citi lifted its Q3 Brent forecast to $80/bbl from $75, noting failed deal attempts, while the US Senate passed a Russia-Iran sanctions bill that could pressure Indian crude imports. Saudi Arabia is routing oil via Yanbu and the SUMED pipeline to sidestep Hormuz at meaningful extra cost.
drivers: Hormuz de-escalation speculation triggered sharp weekly selloff (-8.5% WTI, -8.5% Brent), with RBOB down ~16% on the week
ADNOC flagged 15 vessel attacks impacting operations; $1.3bn supertanker purchase signals Abu Dhabi preparing for prolonged disruption
US Senate passed Russia-Iran sanctions bill; Citi raised Q3 Brent to $80/bbl but still sees 2027 prices lower

gas.summary: Henry Hub edged up 0.76% on the day to $2.66/MMBtu but remains under pressure on a weekly (-3.17%) and monthly (-11.69%) basis, pointing to a soft domestic supply-demand backdrop. TTF dipped 0.46% to €55.51/MWh on the day, though it has outperformed month-on-month (+10.79%), reflecting Europe's ongoing LNG import competition and Hormuz shipping risks. ADNOC's report of 15 vessel attacks and its $1.3 billion carrier acquisition are the most directly relevant gas headlines, as the company is explicitly trying to keep gas as well as crude flowing through a contested corridor. Baker Hughes data showed the US oil-and-gas rig count was flat week-on-week, offering no near-term supply catalyst in either direction. News flow for domestic gas fundamentals is thin today.
drivers: Henry Hub modestly firmer on the day but down sharply on the week and month, signaling soft US domestic fundamentals
ADNOC vessel attacks and supertanker expansion highlight LNG supply-chain risk through the Gulf corridor, supporting TTF's monthly outperformance
US rig count flat week-on-week per Baker Hughes, providing no incremental directional signal for near-term supply

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs were the session's standout performer in this complex, gaining 1.77% to $79.01 and extending gains to +2.60% on the week and +5.73% on the month. The move is notable given TTF's concurrent softness (-0.46% today, -6.03% on the week), as lower gas prices would typically ease fuel-switching pressure and weigh on carbon demand — yet EUAs are rallying regardless, suggesting either speculative positioning or anticipation of tighter policy. Dedicated power-sector headlines are sparse today; the most relevant macro inputs are Iran-related geopolitical noise, including conflicting signals from Washington on whether a Hormuz deal is imminent and whether Iranian supply returns. A Ukraine air-defense deterioration story adds broader European energy-security anxiety. Overall, the EUA move looks technically and macro-driven rather than fundamentally anchored to today's news.
drivers: EUA carbon prices +1.77% on the day and +5.73% on the month, diverging from softer TTF gas — suggests speculative or policy-driven bid rather than fuel-switching dynamics
Conflicting Iran signals (Trump 'winding down' vs. troops being added, permanent Hormuz ban speculation) keep European energy-security risk premium elevated
Ukraine air-defense concerns add peripheral European power-supply anxiety; dedicated power-sector news flow is thin today
